findings.title: Narrowing the exported cache-key helper breaks existing string callers
findings.explanation: `memberCacheKey` previously accepted any `string`, but now requires the nominal `MemberId` type. A caller that already validates or retrieves a member ID as a plain string compiled against the base revision and now fails type-checking, even though the helper’s runtime behavior and accepted value format are unchanged. The PR must either migrate every caller to produce `MemberId` or preserve a compatible boundary that validates and brands the argument. Repository-wide caller verification was unavailable because the read-only command environment could not create its namespace, so confidence is limited to the direct exported-signature incompatibility.

findings.title: Retry loop exceeds `maxAttempts` by one
findings.explanation: With `maxAttempts == 1` and a sender that returns an error, `Deliver` invokes `send` twice and returns an attempt count of 2. The parameter and return value both describe attempts, so the changed `<=` boundary directly violates the declared bound. This can issue an extra dependency request and may duplicate externally committed side effects when an earlier call succeeds remotely but reports an error locally. The caller inventory and tests were unavailable because repository reads were blocked, so a separate undocumented “retry count” contract could not be checked; the supplied current-head hunk nevertheless directly contradicts the function's `maxAttempts` interface.
findings.failurePath: `attempt` starts at 0; for `maxAttempts == 1`, the loop runs at attempts 0 and 1 because `attempt <= maxAttempts`; both failures reach the final return, which reports `maxAttempts + 1` (2). Restore an exclusive upper bound, or rename and document the parameter as a retry count if one initial attempt plus N retries is the intended contract.

findings.title: Preserve the exclusive end of each page
findings.explanation: Array.slice excludes its second argument, so subtracting one makes every full page one item short. For pageSize=1 every nonempty page is empty; for four items with pageSize=2, page 1 omits index 1 and page 2 omits index 3, permanently dropping those items. The exclusive end must remain min(start + pageSize, items.length).
findings.failurePath: pageItems(['a'], 1, 1) computes start=0 and endExclusive=0, then items.slice(0, 0) returns [] instead of ['a'].

findings.title: Exclusive slice boundary permanently drops the last item of every page
findings.explanation: `Array.prototype.slice` already treats its second argument as exclusive, so subtracting one makes every non-empty page one item short. For example, `pageItems(["a"], 1, 1)` now returns `[]`; with `["a","b","c"]` and page size 2, page 1 returns `["a"]` and page 2 returns `["c"]`, meaning `"b"` is never returned. This directly violates contiguous, complete pagination. Restore `Math.min(start + pageSize, items.length)` and cover page size 1, exact-full-page, and one-item-over-boundary cases. Repository caller/test inspection was unavailable because the read-only execution sandbox could not create its namespace, but the authoritative current-head hunk provides direct static proof.
findings.failurePath: A valid positive page and pageSize compute `start`; the changed expression computes `endExclusive = start + pageSize - 1`; `items.slice(start, endExclusive)` excludes that index, returning at most `pageSize - 1` entries. The next page starts at `start + pageSize`, so the omitted item is skipped permanently rather than appearing on a later page.

findings.title: Use the exclusive slice endpoint without subtracting one
findings.explanation: `Array.prototype.slice` already excludes its second argument, so subtracting one removes an additional item from every nonempty requested page. For example, `pageItems(["a", "b"], 1, 2)` now returns only `["a"]`, while `pageItems(["a"], 1, 1)` returns `[]`. This directly breaks full pages, partial final pages, and the minimum valid page size. The two breadth candidates are therefore one root-cause pagination defect. Restore `Math.min(start + pageSize, items.length)` and cover page size 1, an exact full page, and a final partial page.
findings.failurePath: For `page=1` and `pageSize=1`, validation accepts both values, `start` becomes 0, and the changed expression computes `endExclusive` as `Math.min(0, items.length)`, which is 0. `items.slice(0, 0)` then returns an empty array despite an eligible first item. The same off-by-one truncates every nonempty page by one item.

findings.title: Keep the slice endpoint exclusive of exactly pageSize items
findings.explanation: Subtracting one from the exclusive endpoint makes every populated page return at most pageSize - 1 items and permanently skips each page-boundary item. For example, [a,b,c] with pageSize 2 yields [a] for page 1 and [c] for page 2, so b is never returned; with pageSize 1, every page is empty. The previous start + pageSize endpoint already matched Array.slice's exclusive-end contract.
findings.failurePath: Call pageItems([a,b,c], 1, 2); validation passes, start becomes 0, endExclusive becomes 1, and slice(0,1) returns only [a]. The next page starts at index 2, so the omitted item at index 1 cannot appear on any page.

findings.title: Empty SERVICE_PORT now bypasses validation
findings.explanation: The existing contract explicitly distinguishes an absent value, which defaults to 8080, from an empty value, which `test_empty_value_is_rejected` requires to raise `ValueError`. An explicitly empty environment variable is reachable through deployment configuration or template substitution. This change silently binds the service to port 8080 instead and also makes the existing focused test fail. Preserve the absence-only check so only a missing key receives the default.
findings.failurePath: `load_port({"SERVICE_PORT": ""})` reads `raw == ""`; the new truthiness check enters the default branch and returns 8080 before `int(raw)` can reject the malformed value.

findings.title: Do not treat an explicitly empty port as absent

That explicit value previously reached `int(raw)` and failed validation, but the current head silently substitutes port 8080. This can start the service on an unintended port instead of exposing invalid deployment configuration. Preserve the default only for a missing key and add a regression test distinguishing an absent value from an empty one.

findings.title: Retry loop exceeds maxAttempts by one
findings.explanation: The changed inclusive loop treats maxAttempts as a maximum index rather than a maximum count. For Deliver(3, an always-failing Sender), attempt takes values 0 through 3, so send is invoked four times and the function returns 4. The prior implementation, parameter name, and return contract all establish that maxAttempts bounds total invocations. No guard stops the extra call after the third failure. This also affects data-integrity and error-recovery behavior, so the three breadth candidates consolidate into this root cause.
findings.failurePath: Call Deliver(3, send) where send returns an error on every invocation. The loop condition attempt <= maxAttempts permits attempts 0, 1, 2, and 3; every iteration calls send, then exhaustion returns maxAttempts + 1 and the final error. The caller observes four attempted side effects despite configuring a limit of three.

findings.title: The loop exceeds the configured maximum attempt count
findings.explanation: `maxAttempts` denotes the total attempt ceiling, as reflected by the parameter name and the base implementation's `< maxAttempts` bound. Changing the comparison to `<=` invokes `send` once beyond that ceiling: `maxAttempts=1` can send twice, while `maxAttempts=0` now sends once. This can duplicate a side effect and violates callers' configured delivery limit. The changed return value merely reports the extra attempt and does not repair the invariant.
findings.failurePath: Call `Deliver(1, send)` with a sender that fails its first invocation. The loop runs for attempts 0 and 1, so `send` is called twice and the function returns an attempt count of 2, exceeding `maxAttempts`.

findings.title: Restore pointer receivers for both account mutators
findings.explanation: Both methods now receive Account by value, copying balance, held, and the mutex. Credit therefore changes only a temporary copy. Reserve may return true after checking copied state, but its held increment is also discarded. Because each call locks a distinct copied mutex, concurrent operations are not serialized either. One shared repair—restoring pointer receivers—fixes both counterexamples.

findings.explanation: At current head e67aecb30570006dc71001af8dc687f2414a3446, both methods copy Account, including its balance, held amount, and mutex. Credit therefore returns without changing the original balance. Reserve may return true while changing only the copy's held amount, allowing later reservations to reuse the same apparent funds. Copying the mutex also means calls do not synchronize through the account's shared lock. The previous pointer receivers establish the required in-place mutation contract. Restore pointer receivers for both methods and add behavior tests asserting that credits and successful reservations remain visible to subsequent calls.

A subsequent Reserve(80) copies the unchanged original held value of 0 and succeeds again. Likewise, Credit(10) updates only a temporary copy. findings.title: Capacity-one result channel deadlocks batches larger than one
findings.explanation: `Run` starts one producer per job but does not drain `results` until after `workers.Wait()`. With two jobs, the first worker fills the newly capacity-one channel; the second blocks sending and cannot call `Done`, so `Wait` never returns. This regresses the existing contract that `Run` completes with one result per submitted job. Keep capacity sufficient for all producers or consume results concurrently before waiting.
findings.failurePath: Call `Run` with two jobs -> both workers attempt to send -> the first result fills the channel -> the second worker blocks on send -> its deferred `workers.Done()` cannot execute -> `workers.Wait()` blocks before result collection begins -> `Run` hangs indefinitely.

findings.title: Prevent workers from blocking before results are drained
findings.explanation: Every worker sends a result before completing, while Run waits for all workers before it drains the channel. Reducing the buffer to one means that for any batch containing at least two jobs, one result fills the channel and a later worker blocks sending. That worker cannot complete the wait group, so Run remains stuck in Wait and returns none of the results. This single ordering-and-capacity defect also accounts for the result-completeness counterexample.
findings.failurePath: Run receives two jobs → the first worker fills the one-slot results channel → the second worker blocks sending → the blocked worker cannot signal completion → workers.Wait never returns → channel draining is unreachable.

The base implementation validated every line before performing any write, establishing the all-or-nothing behavior this change regresses. Restore a complete validation pass before mutation and add a test asserting unchanged stock after any later line fails.
findings.failurePath: reserve finds the first line valid -> decrements item.available -> a later duplicate or invalid line throws -> the function exits without rollback -> the caller receives an error with partially changed stock.

findings.title: Malformed timestamps bypass lifecycle checks
findings.explanation: Several new lifecycle paths compare Date.parse results without first requiring a finite timestamp. Here, observedAt='not-a-date' produces NaN, making the staleness comparison false; previewReservation consequently accepts the snapshot and can return a successful receipt. The same comparison defect lets an invalid expiresAt pass IdempotencyRegistry.remember and remain forever because lookup and prune also compare NaN, while ReservationStore.transition accepts and persists an invalid updatedAt. Use one required-timestamp parser at these boundaries and test malformed freshness, expiry, and transition timestamps.
findings.failurePath: Date.parse returns NaN -> relational comparison evaluates false -> reservation freshness validation, idempotency expiry rejection/pruning, or monotonic-transition validation is skipped -> invalid state is accepted or retained indefinitely.

findings.title: Invalid receipts corrupt computed availability
findings.explanation: Expected receipt quantities are summed without validation. With available=5 and a qualifying receipt of quantity=-4, queryAvailability reports only 1 unit available by the promise date; fractional or unsafe quantities likewise propagate into the answer. Malformed arrival dates are silently discarded because filtering occurs before validation, a pattern also present in makeInventoryPromise. Validate every receipt's timestamp and nonnegative safe-integer quantity before applying the cutoff, preferably through a shared receipt validator.
findings.failurePath: queryAvailability selects the SKU row -> the cutoff filter admits a negative or otherwise invalid qualifying receipt -> reduce adds its unchecked quantity -> availableByPromiseDate and contributingWarehouses are computed from corrupted inbound stock.

findings.title: Duplicate purchase-order lines are silently overwritten
findings.explanation: Map construction keeps only the last order line for each SKU without rejecting or aggregating duplicates. For order lines A:5 and A:10, a receipt of A:8 is accepted against the latter entry even though it exceeds the former; reversing the input order changes the result. Because the API addresses receipt lines only by SKU, duplicate order entries must be rejected or deliberately aggregated before validation.
findings.failurePath: applyReceipt converts order lines to a Map keyed by SKU -> a later duplicate overwrites the earlier quantity and previouslyReceived state -> receipt validation uses only the surviving line -> acceptance depends on input order and can exceed an order line.

findings.title: Invalid source state can produce negative inventory
findings.explanation: validateTransfer checks the transfer quantity but never validates source or target onHand/reserved values. A source with onHand=0 and reserved=-10 passes the availability expression for a quantity of 5, after which applyTransfer returns source.onHand=-5. The exported validation boundary should require safe, nonnegative stock values and reserved <= onHand before applying the transfer.
findings.failurePath: negative reserved stock inflates source.onHand - source.reserved -> the insufficiency guard passes -> applyTransfer subtracts the quantity from onHand -> a negative source balance is returned as success.

findings.title: Restore the tenant boundary in the approval predicate
findings.explanation: The changed helper now authorizes solely by role and no longer relates the session to the invoice. A billing approver for tenant A therefore receives `true` for an invoice owned by tenant B. Because this exported predicate is the invoice-approval authorization decision, every caller relying on it loses tenant isolation; restoring the shared tenant comparison addresses both the authorization and logic counterexamples.
findings.failurePath: Create a session with `tenantId` A and role `billing-approver`, then pass an invoice with `tenantId` B. `roles.includes("billing-approver")` evaluates true, so `canApproveInvoice` authorizes the cross-tenant invoice and an approval path gated by this result proceeds.

findings.title: Restore the tenant boundary on invoice approval
findings.explanation: At head 9384da5ad9cc58362cba39e57fce7caee86fc426, the shared approval predicate checks only the billing-approver role. A session for tenant A with that role therefore passes an invoice belonging to tenant B. `approveInvoice` has no independent tenant guard: it trusts this predicate and returns `approved:<invoice id>`. This is a reachable cross-tenant authorization bypass and directly regresses the tenant comparison present at the base revision. The authorization and logic candidates consolidate into this single root cause.
findings.failurePath: Create a session with `tenantId: "tenant-a"` and role `billing-approver`, then pass an invoice with `tenantId: "tenant-b"`; `roles.includes` returns true, `canApproveInvoice` authorizes the request, and `approveInvoice` skips its `not authorized` error and reports the foreign invoice as approved.

findings.title: Stale failures can roll back a newer preference mutation
findings.explanation: Removing the mutationId guard allows any failed mutation to restore previousValue and clear saving. This conflicts with applySuccess, which still ignores stale completions. If mutation 1 fails after mutation 2 has updated the same state, mutation 1 now overwrites mutation 2's optimistic value and falsely marks the save complete.
findings.failurePath: Start mutation 1; start mutation 2 before mutation 1 settles; mutation 2 becomes the active state and updates previousValue/value; mutation 1 fails with its older mutationId; applyFailure ignores that ID, restores the active state's previousValue, and sets saving=false while mutation 2 is still pending.

findings.title: Preserve newer state when an older mutation fails
findings.explanation: The removed mutation-ID guard lets an out-of-order failure roll back a newer optimistic update. For example, calling `applyFailure` with mutation ID 1 while the supplied state has `mutationId: 2`, `value: "new"`, and `previousValue: "old"` now returns `value: "old"` and `saving: false`. This can regress the displayed preference and falsely indicate that the active save has finished. If mutation 2 later succeeds, `applySuccess` can even confirm the already-reverted value because its stale-result guard remains but it derives `confirmedValue` from the current state. The exported function still accepts a request-specific mutation ID, and `applySuccess` retains the corresponding identity check, strongly confirming that asynchronous results are intended to apply only to their originating mutation. Restore the same guard in `applyFailure` and cover failure of mutation 1 after mutation 2 has begun. Static verification used the authoritative current-head hunk; repository caller and test inspection was unavailable because read-only command execution was blocked by the namespace sandbox.
findings.failurePath: Begin mutation 1, then begin mutation 2; when mutation 1 rejects, its callback invokes `applyFailure(stateForMutation2, 1)`. The function ignores the ID mismatch, copies `previousValue` over mutation 2's optimistic value, and clears `saving`, allowing the stale callback to overwrite current UI state.

findings.title: First-attempt boundary no longer has regression coverage
findings.explanation: The change removes the attempt=0 case while retaining only attempt=3. A future implementation that incorrectly applies delay on the first attempt would therefore still satisfy this table test. The base test establishes attempt 0 as a reachable case with an expected zero delay. Repository-wide duplicate coverage could not be checked because the command sandbox could not create its namespace, so this is follow-up hardening rather than a blocking correctness finding.
findings.failurePath: Change Delay so attempt 0 returns a nonzero duration; TestDelay now executes only attempt 3 and can pass without observing the first-attempt regression.

findings.title: Restore coverage for the zero-attempt delay branch
findings.explanation: This deletion removes the only assertion for `Delay(0)`, even though `delay.go` handles attempt zero through a distinct early-return branch. No equivalent test exists elsewhere in the package. If that branch later returns a positive duration, the remaining attempt-3 case still passes while every initial retry can be unnecessarily delayed.
findings.failurePath: A retry starts with attempt 0; the dedicated branch in `Delay` regresses to a nonzero result; the suite exercises only attempt 3 and passes; the caller observes an incorrect initial delay.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping for workspace management
findings.explanation: The shared `canManage` helper now checks only `workspace:manage`, removing the base revision's actor/workspace tenant comparison. Consequently, any actor holding that permission can read another tenant's `secret` through `readSecret` and modify another tenant's `setting` through `updateSetting`. Because both paths rely on this helper, restoring the tenant comparison here addresses both disclosure and mutation.
findings.failurePath: Create an actor for tenant A with `workspace:manage` and pass a workspace owned by tenant B. `canManage(actor)` returns true, so `readSecret` returns tenant B's secret and `updateSetting` returns tenant B's workspace with the attacker-selected setting.

findings.title: Preserve tenant isolation in workspace management
findings.explanation: The shared authorization helper now checks only `workspace:manage` and no longer verifies that `actor.tenantId` matches `workspace.tenantId`. Consequently, an actor with that permission for tenant A can read the secret or update the setting of any tenant B workspace supplied to these exported functions. Both operations previously enforced the tenant boundary, so this is a direct authorization regression at the reviewed head. Restore the workspace-aware tenant check in the shared helper and cover cross-tenant reads and mutations, including asserting unchanged foreign state after a denied update. Repository inspection was unavailable because the sandbox could not create its execution namespace; the authoritative changed hunk nevertheless provides direct static proof.
findings.failurePath: A caller passes an actor with `workspace:manage` and `tenantId = A` together with a workspace whose `tenantId = B`; `canManage(actor)` returns true based solely on permission, `readSecret` returns the foreign workspace secret, and `updateSetting` returns the foreign workspace with an attacker-selected setting instead of throwing `not authorized`.

findings.title: Keep production file-handler INFO records reachable
findings.explanation: Every new production profile sets the logger level to WARNING while configuring its file handler at INFO. Both the root and `service` logger therefore reject INFO records before handler dispatch, so the advertised file threshold is ineffective across all production profiles.
findings.failurePath: Load any `*-production` profile, apply the rendered dictionary, then emit an INFO record through `service`, its descendants, or a logger inheriting from root; the record is discarded before the INFO file handler can write it.

findings.title: Avoid attaching the same handlers on both propagation paths
findings.explanation: The renderer attaches every handler to both `service` and root. All new development profiles enable propagation, so a record accepted by `service` is handled there and then handled again by root, producing duplicate console output. This systemic renderer issue affects every development profile.
findings.failurePath: Load any `*-development` profile, apply the configuration, and emit one record from `service` or a descendant; the service handler emits it once and propagation invokes the same handler again from root.

findings.title: Re-export the legacy validation constants
findings.explanation: Before the refactor, `VALID_LEVELS` and `VALID_FORMATS` were public module attributes and were included by wildcard imports. The compatibility wrapper neither imports nor lists them, despite preserving the other legacy symbols, so existing direct or wildcard imports now fail or lose those names.
findings.failurePath: A consumer importing `VALID_LEVELS` or `VALID_FORMATS` from `logging_config` upgrades to this revision and fails during module import with `ImportError`.

findings.title: Compatibility shim drops the public level and format constants
findings.explanation: The base module publicly defined `VALID_LEVELS` and `VALID_FORMATS`, but the replacement shim imports neither name. Existing consumers using `from logging_config import VALID_LEVELS, VALID_FORMATS` now fail during import. This contradicts the shim's demonstrated compatibility role and should be fixed by re-exporting the existing constants from `logsettings.parsing`.
findings.failurePath: Python resolves the requested attribute on `logging_config`; because the shim never imports either constant, import processing raises `ImportError` before the consumer can start.

findings.title: The shared logger graph duplicates development logs and suppresses production file INFO logs
findings.explanation: The renderer attaches every handler to both `service` and root while independently enabling propagation. Across all development profiles, an INFO record from `service` is handled locally and then propagated to the same root handler, producing two identical emissions. Across all production profiles, the `service` and root levels are WARNING even though the file handler is INFO, so an INFO record is rejected by the logger before that file handler can receive it. Canary and staging avoid duplication because propagation is false. The shared renderer should establish one handler ownership point and set the logger threshold low enough for the least-restrictive configured handler.
findings.failurePath: Development: `service.info()` passes the INFO logger threshold, invokes its console handler, propagates, and invokes the same handler through root. Production: `service.info()` fails the service logger's WARNING threshold, so dispatch never reaches the file handler configured for INFO.

findings.title: JSON profiles emit malformed records for ordinary message content
findings.explanation: The JSON formatter interpolates `%(message)s` directly inside quoted JSON. A reachable message such as `logger.info('user="alice"')`, a newline, or a backslash is inserted without JSON escaping, yielding invalid output. Every canary, staging, and production profile selects this formatter, so downstream JSON log ingestion can reject or misparse otherwise successful records. Use a formatter that serializes a record object through a JSON encoder.
findings.failurePath: A caller emits a message containing a JSON-special character; `logging.Formatter` substitutes the raw message into the format literal, and the handler writes syntactically invalid JSON to its configured sink.

findings.title: Validate the complete reservation before mutating stock
findings.explanation: At the reviewed head, validation and mutation occur in the same loop. With stock A=5 and B=0, reserving A=2 followed by B=1 decrements A to 3 before throwing for B. The base implementation completed a validation pass first, so this is a direct regression that leaves rejected requests partially applied.
findings.failurePath: reserve([A:2,B:1]) -> validate A -> decrement A -> validate B -> throw -> caller observes A mutated despite failure

findings.title: Order timestamps by parsed instants rather than their text
findings.explanation: Several new helpers accept offset-bearing timestamps but order them with localeCompare. For example, 2024-01-01T01:00:00+02:00 is earlier than 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z despite sorting after it lexically. In projectStock this can process a reservation before its receipt and reject a valid history. The same comparison policy misorders cycle-count due dates, audit history/latest selection, expiry batches, reservation and quarantine listings, and equal-expiry lot receipt order.
findings.failurePath: valid offset timestamps -> lexical sort in projectStock (also cycle-count:43, inventory-audit:28/45, reservation-expiry:35, reservation-store:49, quarantine-service:34, lot-selection:20) -> operations run in the wrong chronological order

findings.title: Reject malformed timestamps before temporal comparisons
findings.explanation: Date.parse failures produce NaN, and the changed code compares that value without checking finiteness. An idempotency record with expiresAt="not-a-date" passes remember, is never expired by lookup or prune, and can replay indefinitely. The same pattern accepts an invalid stock observedAt in reservation-policy.ts:39 and persists an invalid transition updatedAt in reservation-store.ts:43.
findings.failurePath: malformed timestamp -> Date.parse returns NaN -> <=, >, or < comparison evaluates false -> invalid record, snapshot, or transition is accepted

findings.title: Validate expected receipts before adding them to availability
findings.explanation: The function validates current availability but adds receipt quantities without validating them. A matching receipt with quantity=-100 reduces availableByPromiseDate, while fractional or infinite values can produce invalid promise totals. This contradicts the validation applied to the same inbound-quantity concept in makeInventoryPromise.
findings.failurePath: matching expected receipt -> arrival filter succeeds -> unchecked quantity enters reduce -> corrupted availableByPromiseDate drives canPromise and availabilityRatio

findings.title: Reject invalid lot quantities before allocation
findings.explanation: Eligibility checks only available > 0. Two eligible lots with available=0.5 can satisfy an integer request for one unit by returning two fractional allocations; an infinite value can satisfy demand using invalid stock. The requested quantity is explicitly constrained to inventory units, so accepting non-integer lot stock breaks the allocation contract.
findings.failurePath: fractional or infinite lot availability -> passes available > 0 -> Math.min emits an allocation from invalid stock -> request can complete with invalid lot quantities

findings.title: Reject duplicate and invalid purchase-order lines before receiving
findings.explanation: Map construction silently overwrites duplicate order SKUs and no validation is applied to ordered or previouslyReceived. With duplicate SKU lines ordered for 10 and 100 units, the latter wins and a 50-unit receipt is accepted even though it exceeds the first authoritative-looking line. Malformed numeric order state can similarly bypass the over-receipt comparison.
findings.failurePath: duplicate or malformed purchase-order lines -> Map keeps the last line -> receipt is checked against overwritten or invalid limits -> excess or corrupt receipt is returned as applied

findings.title: Validate reservation event fields before serialization
findings.explanation: The serializer checks only that the line array is nonempty. A line with quantity=NaN is accepted and JSON.stringify publishes it as quantity:null; zero and negative quantities and malformed occurredAt values are also emitted. This produces payloads that contradict the declared InventoryReservedEvent and reservation quantity contracts.
findings.failurePath: invalid event field -> only nonempty-lines guard runs -> JSON.stringify coerces or preserves invalid data -> downstream consumer receives a contract-invalid reservation event

findings.title: Canonicalize existing registry keys before uniqueness checks
findings.explanation: Only additions are normalized. If existing contains key "abc123", registering serial " ABC123 " checks for "ABC123", does not find the lowercase key, and returns both logical copies. The Map type exposes no invariant requiring callers to have canonicalized its existing keys.
findings.failurePath: noncanonical existing key -> shallow Map copy preserves it -> normalized addition is checked under a different key -> duplicate logical serial is inserted

findings.title: Validate package and carrier-rate values before selecting a rate
findings.explanation: Package weights and carrier-rate capacities, prices, and lead times are used without numeric validation. A shipment whose only package has weightGrams=-1 can qualify for a rate and return a successful plan; a negative price can also produce a negative total. These are invalid physical and monetary results, not merely suboptimal selection.
findings.failurePath: invalid package or rate numbers -> heaviest and eligibility calculations accept them -> sort selects the malformed rate -> successful ShipmentPlan contains an invalid cost or is based on impossible weight

findings.title: Validate source and target stock before transfer arithmetic
findings.explanation: validateTransfer checks the transfer quantity but not either stock record. A source with onHand=-1 and reserved=-2 has one apparently transferable unit, so a transfer of one passes and returns source.onHand=-2. Non-integer and non-finite states can likewise propagate corrupt stock while the operation reports success.
findings.failurePath: invalid WarehouseStock -> onHand-reserved comparison appears sufficient -> applyTransfer subtracts quantity -> negative or non-finite stock is returned

findings.title: Validate supplier minimums and lead times before ranking offers
findings.explanation: The function validates price and orderMultiple but omits minimumQuantity and leadTimeDays. For a matching offer with minimumQuantity=NaN, Math.max and subsequent arithmetic produce NaN, yet the sole candidate is selected and returned with quantity and totalPriceCents both NaN. Invalid lead times also make ordering nondeterministic.
findings.failurePath: malformed offer -> partial field validation passes -> quantity or comparator becomes NaN -> candidate remains selectable -> invalid SupplierOrderLine is returned

findings.title: Apply zone capacity validation when calculating utilization
findings.explanation: warehouseZoneUtilization bypasses zoneRemainingUnits, the module's canonical capacity validator. A matching zone with maximumUnits=-1 returns negative utilization, while occupiedUnits greater than maximumUnits returns a value above one instead of rejecting the invalid warehouse state.
findings.failurePath: invalid matching zone -> raw maximumUnits and occupiedUnits are reduced -> division proceeds without zoneRemainingUnits validation -> invalid utilization is returned

findings.title: Reject replenishment rules for a different SKU
findings.explanation: Both StockPosition and ReplenishmentRule carry a SKU, but recommendReplenishment never compares them. A low-stock position for SKU A can therefore be calculated using SKU B's lead time, safety stock, MOQ, and order multiple, while the result is labeled as SKU A.
findings.failurePath: position.sku differs from rule.sku -> no identity check -> rule B parameters calculate position A recommendation -> mislabeled procurement quantity is returned

findings.title: Reject a NaN stockout threshold
findings.explanation: The range check accepts NaN because both comparisons are false. stockoutSkus(metrics, NaN) then silently returns an empty list, even though NaN is outside the intended zero-to-one threshold domain.
findings.failurePath: threshold=NaN -> range guard evaluates false -> every stockoutRate >= NaN comparison is false -> empty result is reported as valid

findings.title: Reservation failure leaves earlier stock mutations committed
findings.explanation: The PR moved each decrement into the validation loop, removing the previous validate-then-commit behavior. A multi-line reservation is therefore no longer atomic: if a later line is invalid, earlier lines remain decremented even though reserve throws and produces no successful reservation. This is a direct regression in the modified method and must be repaired in this PR.
findings.failurePath: Given stock A=5 and B=0, reserve(A:1, B:1) decrements A to 4, then throws for B. A retry or subsequent request observes one unit missing despite the original reservation having failed.

findings.title: Invalid timestamps bypass multiple newly added lifecycle checks
findings.explanation: Several validation paths compare Date.parse results without first requiring a finite timestamp. Here, an invalid snapshot observedAt produces NaN, making the stale comparison false and allowing unverified stock into a reservation. The same root cause lets IdempotencyRegistry.remember store an invalid expiresAt that lookup and prune never expire, and lets ReservationStore.transition accept an invalid updatedAt because its backward-time comparison is also false. A shared required-instant validator would close all three counterexamples.
findings.failurePath: A snapshot with observedAt="not-a-date" passes validateReservationRequest and can authorize a reservation. Separately, an idempotency record with expiresAt="not-a-date" remains active indefinitely, while a transition with updatedAt="not-a-date" permanently records an invalid lifecycle timestamp.

findings.title: Lexical timestamp ordering reverses valid event chronology
findings.explanation: The code accepts any Date-compatible timestamp representation but orders timestamps as strings. Offset-bearing ISO timestamps can sort opposite to their actual instants. This can corrupt or spuriously reject stock projections. The same comparison policy appears in dueForExpiry, where it can select a later expiry ahead of an earlier one under the batch limit, and in inventory audit ordering. Comparing parsed instants through one shared policy addresses these counterexamples.
findings.failurePath: A receipt at 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z occurs before a reservation at 2025-12-31T23:30:00-01:00, but lexical sorting applies the reservation first and throws because reserved exceeds on-hand. With those values as expiry timestamps, dueForExpiry(..., limit=1) likewise chooses the later instant first.

findings.title: Numeric coercion merges distinct customer IDs
findings.explanation: The validator accepts both zero-padded and unpadded identifiers, but converting them through Number makes values such as "00123" and "123" share the key "123". indexCustomers then constructs a Map with that key and silently replaces the first customer with the second, reducing two valid records to one and making lookups return the wrong customer. The previous implementation preserved these identities, and no duplicate guard prevents the overwrite. Preserve the validated string representation, or explicitly reject canonicalization collisions before indexing, with a regression test asserting both records remain independently addressable.

findings.title: Ignore failures from superseded preference mutations
findings.explanation: Removing the mutationId guard allows an older request failure to overwrite state owned by a newer mutation. For example, mutation 1 starts, mutation 2 updates the preference and becomes current, then mutation 1 fails: applyFailure rolls value back to previousValue and clears saving even though mutation 2 remains active. The adjacent applySuccess guard confirms that mutation IDs define completion ordering and stale completions must be ignored. This visibly discards the user's newer selection and may let mutation 2 subsequently confirm the regressed value.
findings.failurePath: Older request rejects -> applyFailure receives the current state and older mutationId -> no mutationId comparison occurs -> current value is replaced with previousValue and saving becomes false -> the newer optimistic preference disappears while its request is still active.

findings.title: Reject failures from superseded mutations
findings.explanation: `usePreference.setValue` permits overlapping saves and assigns each one a mutation ID. After `beginSave("weekly")` and `beginSave("monthly")`, a late failure from the weekly request now rolls the current state back to `weekly` and clears `saving`, even though the monthly request is newer or already confirmed. This makes the rendered value disagree with `confirmedValue`; if the newer success arrives afterward, `applySuccess` can even confirm the rolled-back value rather than the value actually saved. Restore the mutation-ID guard and retain the out-of-order failure regression test. Static proof is complete, but runtime execution was unavailable.

Request 1 then rejects and dispatches failure ID 1. `applyFailure` ignores that ID, assigns `value=previousValue` (`"weekly"`), and sets `saving=false`, overwriting mutation 2's state.

findings.title: Preserve an explicit zero-second shutdown grace
findings.explanation: Replacing the explicit `is not None` check with truthiness makes the valid value `cli_grace=0` behave as though the CLI option was omitted. The function’s `int | None` contract and the remaining `< 0` validation show that zero is accepted while `None` is the omission sentinel. Consequently, `resolve_config(0, {"SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS":"30"})` returns 30 instead of 0; it can also raise while parsing an invalid environment value that should have been ignored because the CLI supplied a valid value. Both counterexamples have the same root cause and are repaired by restoring an explicit `None` comparison.
findings.failurePath: Caller requests immediate shutdown with `cli_grace=0` -> `cli_grace or ...` evaluates the environment branch -> the environment value replaces zero (or fails integer parsing) -> the worker does not honor the explicit CLI configuration.

findings.title: Explicit zero shutdown grace is overwritten by the environment
findings.explanation: The changed truthiness fallback conflates an explicit CLI value of 0 with an absent value. `resolve_config(0, {"SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS":"30"})` now returns 30, while the base implementation returned 0. Zero is supported by the function contract and unchanged validation, which rejects only negative values. No guard excludes zero before this expression. A malformed environment value can also now raise during `int(...)` despite the valid CLI override. Preserve the explicit `is not None` precedence check.
findings.failurePath: Caller supplies `cli_grace=0` → `cli_grace or ...` treats it as false → the environment value is parsed → configuration returns that value or raises instead of honoring the CLI override.

findings.title: Fractional offsets can now discard an item before slicing
findings.explanation: The exported function accepts unrestricted `number` arguments, but the new raw-value comparison is not equivalent to `Array.prototype.slice` normalization. For `windowItems(['a'], 0.5, 0.5)`, the previous implementation evaluated `slice(0.5, 1)` and returned `['a']`; the current head computes `lastIndex = 0`, takes `0 < 0.5`, and returns `[]`. No integer validation or integer-only type guards this path in the changed helper. Preserve the original slice semantics or explicitly validate/normalize offset and limit before calculating and comparing indices; add a regression test covering fractional boundaries.
findings.failurePath: A caller supplies offset 0.5 and limit 0.5 -> `lastIndex` becomes 0 -> the early-return predicate compares unnormalized values and returns `[]` -> the item that `slice(0.5, 1)` would include is omitted.

findings.title: Direct checkpoint writes destroy the last valid checkpoint on failure
findings.explanation: `save_checkpoint` now opens the destination itself with mode `w`, truncating any existing checkpoint before invoking the injectable writer. A reachable counterexample is a writer that writes part of the JSON and then raises: the exception propagates, but the prior valid checkpoint has already been replaced by partial contents. The same exposure exists if the process is interrupted during serialization. The removed temporary-file-plus-`os.replace` path preserved the previous checkpoint until serialization completed, so this is a current-head regression in checkpoint recovery behavior. Restore write-to-temporary followed by atomic replacement, with temporary-file cleanup on failure.
findings.failurePath: An existing valid checkpoint is present -> `path.open("w")` immediately truncates it -> `writer(stream, value)` writes partially and raises or the process stops -> the context closes or the process exits without restoring the old contents -> the next reader observes an incomplete checkpoint and cannot recover the last valid state. Static verification is conclusive from the authoritative hunk; repository inspection was unavailable because the execution sandbox could not initialize.

findings.title: Preserve the last valid checkpoint during writes
findings.explanation: Opening the checkpoint itself with "w" truncates the previously valid file before serialization completes. If the injectable writer raises after writing nothing or only part of the JSON, or the process is interrupted mid-write, the checkpoint becomes empty or malformed. The removed temporary-file-and-replace path kept the prior checkpoint intact until a complete replacement was ready.
findings.failurePath: An existing valid checkpoint is opened for saving -> open("w") immediately truncates it -> writer raises or execution stops before completing valid JSON -> save fails while the prior checkpoint has already been destroyed -> the next recovery attempt reads an empty or malformed checkpoint.

findings.title: Superseded search responses can overwrite current results
findings.explanation: The removed requestId guard was the only shown check tying a response to state.latestRequestId. If search 1 begins, then search 2 begins, response 2 is accepted, and response 1 arrives afterward, response 1 now replaces the newer items and clears loading. Network completion order therefore determines the visible result set. This remains present in the authoritative diff at head 4f57c8a901982409e1f19ed85ec8a012f32aa034 and directly contradicts the latestRequestId sequencing model. Restore the identity check at this shared acceptance boundary and cover the out-of-order completion case.
findings.failurePath: beginSearch records request 2 as latestRequestId -> response 2 is accepted -> delayed response 1 reaches acceptSearchResponse -> no requestId comparison runs -> response 1 items overwrite response 2 items and loading becomes false.

findings.title: Stale responses can overwrite the latest search results
findings.explanation: Removing the requestId comparison makes response arrival order determine the visible state. The existing latestRequestId field and response requestId form the freshness boundary: after search B supersedes search A, a delayed response from A is now accepted, replacing B's items and clearing loading. The logic-correctness, data-integrity, and ordering candidates are the same systemic regression and require one repair: restore the freshness guard before applying a response.
findings.failurePath: beginSearch(state, A) -> beginSearch(state, B) -> response B is accepted -> delayed response A is accepted despite A !== latestRequestId -> A's items replace B's items and loading becomes false

findings.title: Validate the destination before debiting the source
findings.explanation: A locked destination is an explicitly reachable input, but this change moves its validation after the first balance mutation. Consequently, a transfer that reports failure corrupts the ledger and violates balance conservation. The logic-correctness and error-recovery candidates share this single root cause; restoring validation before mutation covers both.
findings.failurePath: Given a source balance of 1000, a `locked-` destination balance of 200, and a transfer of 300, the preliminary checks pass. Line 13 reduces the source to 700, line 14 throws `destination locked`, and the destination credit never executes. The caller retains the mutated Map with balances [700, 200] despite the failed transfer.

findings.title: Validate the destination before debiting the source account
findings.explanation: At head 24fd2c58a913dd2330b4d706a514c9f40e51fcb7, a transfer with sufficient funds to an existing account whose ID starts with `locked-` debits the source and then throws before crediting the destination. This reachable error path turns a rejected transfer into permanent in-memory balance loss and directly regresses the base behavior, which checked the destination before mutation. Move the locked-destination check back before either balance update and add a regression test asserting that both balances remain unchanged after the rejection. Repository inspection was unavailable because the read-only shell sandbox could not create its namespace, but the authoritative changed hunk provides a direct static contradiction.
findings.failurePath: `accounts.get` resolves both accounts → the funds check passes → `from.balanceCents -= cents` mutates the source → the locked-destination predicate matches → the function throws `destination locked` → the destination is never credited and no rollback restores the source.

findings.title: Direct writes can destroy the last valid checkpoint
findings.explanation: Opening the destination with `"w"` truncates the existing checkpoint before `writer` succeeds. The injectable writer can raise after writing nothing or only part of the JSON, and ordinary I/O failures can do the same. The context manager closes the stream but cannot restore the previous contents. The removed temporary-file plus `os.replace` flow explicitly provided this atomic-replacement guarantee, so this change introduces a reachable data-loss regression.
findings.failurePath: Given an existing valid checkpoint, call `save_checkpoint` with a writer that writes partially and raises. `path.open("w")` first truncates the destination, the writer then fails, and the exception propagates while the checkpoint remains empty or malformed instead of retaining its prior valid value.

findings.title: Preserve the last valid checkpoint until the replacement is complete
findings.explanation: Opening the checkpoint itself with mode "w" truncates the previously valid value before serialization succeeds. If the injected writer raises after a partial write, or the process is interrupted during serialization, the checkpoint is left empty or malformed. The removed temporary-file plus os.replace flow is direct evidence that checkpoint replacement was intentionally atomic and that serialization failures were expected to preserve the old file.
findings.failurePath: A valid checkpoint exists → save_checkpoint opens it with "w" and immediately truncates it → writer writes partially and raises or the process terminates → no valid old or new checkpoint remains for recovery.

findings.title: Leading-zero IDs collapse onto other valid customer IDs
findings.explanation: The validator accepts any 1–12 digit string, including both "001" and "1", but the new Number conversion normalizes both to "1". This makes two accepted external identifiers indistinguishable and can cause customer-index collisions or incorrect lookup results. Preserve the validated representation unless the contract explicitly defines external IDs as canonical integers; otherwise reject non-canonical forms before indexing.
findings.failurePath: A caller supplies records identified by "001" and "1". Both inputs pass the unchanged validation, normalize to the same Map key "1", and therefore cannot remain independently addressable when indexed.

findings.title: Preserve distinct valid external IDs
findings.explanation: The validator accepts leading-zero IDs, but the Number/String round-trip collapses them: `"001"` and `"1"` both normalize to `"1"`, while `"000"` becomes `"0"`. This silently changes valid external identifiers and can make distinct customer records share an index key, causing one record to replace another. Preserve the validated string unless leading-zero equivalence is explicitly enforced throughout the identifier contract.
findings.failurePath: Two customers have external IDs `001` and `1` → both inputs pass validation → both normalize to `1` → indexing by the normalized value stores both under one Map key → one customer record becomes unreachable or resolves as the other customer.

findings.title: Preserve successful empty-body DELETE responses
findings.explanation: This now calls `response.json()` for every successful response. A valid 204 No Content response has no JSON body, so parsing it raises a decode exception even though the widget was successfully deleted. Callers therefore observe failure after a completed mutation and may retry it. The removed 204 branch was the guard preserving this response contract.
findings.failurePath: `transport.delete()` returns HTTP 204 -> the non-2xx guard is bypassed -> `response.json()` parses the empty body -> a JSON decode exception escapes instead of returning success.

findings.title: Preserve successful 204 DELETE handling
findings.explanation: The removed 204 branch was the only guard preventing JSON parsing on a successful response with no content. A transport response with status 204 and an empty body now passes the 2xx check and reaches `response.json()`, which raises a JSON-decoding exception. The deletion has succeeded, but the client reports failure. This is a direct regression in the changed DELETE contract and should be restored in this PR. The same root cause accounts for the data-integrity and logic-correctness symptoms, so they do not warrant separate findings. Static verification is sufficient from the current-head control flow and 204 No Content semantics; package-script execution was prohibited.
findings.failurePath: `ApiClient.delete_widget(widget_id)` calls `transport.delete`; a 204 response passes the status-range guard; execution falls through to `response.json()` at line 19; parsing the empty body raises instead of returning normally after the successful deletion.

findings.title: Stale failures now roll back the active mutation
findings.explanation: `applyFailure` no longer checks the supplied mutation ID against `state.mutationId`, while the unchanged sibling `applySuccess` still rejects stale completions. For two overlapping saves, mutation 1 can fail after mutation 2 has started; applying that callback to the current state restores mutation 1's `previousValue` and sets `saving` false even though mutation 2 remains active. This violates async ordering, visibly reverts the newer optimistic value, and hides its saving indicator. The three breadth candidates consolidate to this one root invariant. Static proof is direct from the authoritative current-head hunk; caller/test inspection was unavailable, so confidence is reduced from Confirmed.
findings.failurePath: Start mutation 1, then start mutation 2 so state.mutationId identifies mutation 2; mutation 1's failure callback calls `applyFailure(currentState, mutation1Id)`; because `_mutationId` is ignored, the reducer returns `value: state.previousValue, saving: false` instead of leaving mutation 2's state unchanged.

findings.title: Preserve the mutation freshness check on failure
findings.explanation: `usePreference.setValue` permits overlapping saves and dispatches each completion with its mutation ID, so responses can arrive out of order. By ignoring that ID, a late failure from save A unconditionally applies rollback state belonging to save B. If B already succeeded, A restores B's `previousValue`, reverting the displayed preference. If B is still pending, A also clears `saving` and changes `value`; B's later success then confirms that stale value even though the server saved B's requested value. These are manifestations of the same missing freshness guard and should be repaired together by rejecting failures whose mutation ID is no longer current.
findings.failurePath: Begin save A, begin save B, then reject A after B becomes current. The failure action reaches `applyFailure`, which no longer compares its ID with `state.mutationId`, so it restores `previousValue` and clears `saving`, overwriting B's state. The focused state-transition test encodes this reachable ordering and the supplied proof artifact records base exit 0 versus head exit 1; runtime execution was unavailable during this review.

findings.title: Single-slot result channel deadlocks multi-job batches
findings.explanation: Each job runs in its own goroutine and sends one result, but Run waits for every worker before it begins draining the channel. With two or more jobs, the first result fills this new single-slot buffer and another worker blocks while sending, so it cannot call workers.Done(). The wait therefore never returns, Run hangs, and the existing three-job completion test times out. Retain capacity for every pending result or drain concurrently with production.
findings.failurePath: Run receives at least two jobs -> one worker fills results -> another blocks on results <- Result -> workers.Wait waits for that blocked worker -> the receive loop after Wait is never reached.

findings.title: Capacity-one result channel deadlocks batches with multiple jobs
findings.explanation: Run launches one result-producing worker per job but waits for every worker before draining the results channel. After this change, the first result fills the sole buffer slot and the next worker blocks on its send, preventing the WaitGroup from completing. Any batch containing at least two jobs can therefore hang indefinitely instead of returning its results. Keep capacity sufficient for all pre-wait sends, or consume results concurrently with the wait.
findings.failurePath: Call Run with two jobs -> both workers attempt to send -> one result occupies the capacity-one channel -> the other worker blocks sending and cannot call Done -> workers.Wait() never returns -> result collection is never reached.

findings.title: Do not report acceptance when persistence fails
findings.explanation: The new catch converts every rejection from `store.persist(id)` into the same 202 result returned after successful persistence. A caller therefore receives an accepted response even though the import was never stored, while the original failure is discarded. This single root cause violates data integrity, response-contract, and recovery guarantees. The smallest safe repair is to propagate or explicitly map the persistence error and reserve 202 for a successfully persisted import.
findings.failurePath: Call `acceptImport` with an `ImportStore` whose `persist` promise rejects, such as during a database outage. At head `2e7d8bd81ae2beb2482ec5ebf2aed5131b34a8e4`, the rejection enters the new catch and the function returns 202 without persisting `id`, retrying, logging, or signaling failure to its caller.

findings.title: Do not report failed persistence as an accepted import
findings.explanation: When `store.persist(id)` rejects, this catch returns the same 202 used for success. The caller `processImport` therefore continues to `queue.enqueue(id)` and returns 202 even though the import was never persisted. This breaks the existing contract test requiring persistence failures to reject and leave the indexing queue unchanged, and can enqueue an ID with no durable import behind it.
findings.failurePath: Call `processImport` with a store whose `persist` rejects. `acceptImport` catches the rejection and resolves with 202; `processImport` then enqueues the ID and resolves with 202 instead of propagating the persistence failure.

findings.title: Preserve hyphenated account IDs when parsing shipment keys
findings.explanation: Valid keys can contain hyphens within the account component. For `us-acme-retail-0042`, `split("-")` produces four segments, but the new three-element destructuring ignores `0042` and returns `{ region: "us", account: "acme", sequence: "retail" }`. The unchanged validation accepts this corrupted result. The base implementation explicitly preserved this grammar by taking the first segment as region, the last as sequence, and joining all intervening segments as account. The immediate `routingKey` caller therefore emits `us/acme/retail` instead of `us/acme-retail/0042`. This parsing regression is introduced by the PR and should be repaired here.
findings.failurePath: routingKey("us-acme-retail-0042") -> parseShipmentKey -> three-element destructuring drops the final segment -> validation passes -> routingKey returns the wrong account and sequence

findings.title: Preserve hyphenated account identifiers when parsing shipment keys
findings.explanation: The destructuring rewrite changes the established key grammar. For `us-acme-west-42`, the base implementation produced `{region:"us", account:"acme-west", sequence:"42"}`, while the new implementation produces `{region:"us", account:"acme", sequence:"west"}` and silently discards `42`. Hyphenated accounts were explicitly preserved by the removed `parts.join("-")`, so such inputs are reachable under the pre-change contract. This can select the wrong account and sequence instead of rejecting the key, breaking shipment lookup or mutation behavior. Parse the first component as the region, the last as the sequence, and join all intervening components as the account.
findings.failurePath: `value.split("-")` returns four or more components; three-element destructuring binds only the first three and ignores the remainder; the non-empty validation passes; the function returns a truncated account and a non-final sequence.

findings.title: Preserve an explicit zero-second shutdown grace
findings.explanation: The changed truthiness fallback treats `cli_grace=0` as absent, even though the function's contract distinguishes absence with `None` and rejects only negative values. For example, `resolve_config(0, {"SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS":"30"})` now returns a 30-second grace instead of the explicitly requested zero-second grace. This remains present in the authoritative current-head hunk. Restore the explicit `is not None` check and cover zero, `None`, and negative inputs in a focused regression test.
findings.failurePath: A caller supplies CLI grace `0` -> `cli_grace or ...` evaluates the environment fallback -> `SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` is parsed as `30` -> validation accepts it -> `WorkerConfig.shutdown_grace_seconds` becomes `30`, changing shutdown behavior from immediate to delayed.

findings.title: Preserve an explicit zero-second CLI grace period
findings.explanation: The function's type and validation establish that 0 is valid: only None denotes an omitted CLI value, while values below 0 are rejected. Using truthiness treats 0 as absent and incorrectly replaces it with the environment value or the 30-second default.
findings.failurePath: Calling resolve_config(0, {"SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS": "30"}) now returns shutdown_grace_seconds=30 instead of 0; with no environment setting it likewise returns 30.

findings.title: Restore atomic reservation validation
findings.explanation: Moving the decrement into the validation loop makes a rejected reservation partially mutate inventory. The previous two-pass implementation validated every line before changing any stock. This regression can permanently reduce availability even though the caller receives an error.
findings.failurePath: With A.available=5 and B.available=0, reserve([A:1,B:1]) decrements A to 4, then throws for B; the failed reservation retains A's mutation.

findings.title: Reject invalid timestamps before lifecycle comparisons
findings.explanation: Several new validation boundaries use one-sided comparisons on unchecked Date.parse results. Here an invalid expiresAt produces NaN, bypasses the expiry check, and creates a record that lookup and prune never expire. The same systemic comparison defect treats invalid snapshot observedAt values as fresh in reservation-policy.ts and lets invalid updatedAt values bypass chronology checks in reservation-store.ts. A shared strict timestamp parser would cover these counterexamples.
findings.failurePath: remember() accepts expiresAt="invalid" because NaN <= nowMs is false; subsequent lookup() and prune() make the same false comparison, so the idempotency response remains active indefinitely.

findings.title: Allow signed stock adjustments
findings.explanation: The projector requires every movement quantity to be positive and always adds adjustment quantities to on-hand stock. However, reconcileCount() in this PR explicitly emits negative deltas for count shortages. Consequently, a legitimate shortage cannot be projected: passing its delta throws, while converting it to a positive quantity would increase stock instead of decreasing it.
findings.failurePath: A system count of 10 and physical count of 8 yields delta=-2 and reason=count-shortage; representing that as an adjustment movement causes projectStock() to reject the quantity before updating onHand.

findings.title: Validate the complete reservation before mutating stock
findings.explanation: The changed single-pass loop fixes cumulative deductions for repeated SKUs but removes the previous preflight boundary. With stock A=5 and lines [{A,1},{missing,1}], A is decremented to 4 before the second line throws. The caller therefore observes failure while retaining a partial reservation. No rollback or copied working state disconfirms this path.
findings.failurePath: reserve processes the valid first line and immediately decrements item.available; the later stock.get returns undefined and throws, leaving the earlier Map mutation in place. Validate against a temporary cumulative allocation first, then commit only after every line succeeds.

findings.title: Normalize and validate timestamps before ordering or lifecycle comparisons
findings.explanation: Timestamp handling is systemically inconsistent. projectStock orders raw strings, so a receipt at 2026-01-01T10:00:00+01:00 (09:00Z) sorts after a reservation at 09:30Z and throws an invalid projection. The same raw-string ordering selects incorrect audit entries and expiry batches in inventory-audit.ts and reservation-expiry.ts. Separately, Date.parse failures are used without finite checks in idempotency.ts, reservation-policy.ts, and reservation-store.ts: an invalid expiry is stored indefinitely, an invalid observedAt passes freshness validation, and an invalid updatedAt is persisted. These inputs are reachable because the public interfaces accept strings, while existing validators explicitly accept any parseable offset timestamp. A shared parse-and-validate boundary returning epoch values covers the affected comparisons.
findings.failurePath: Raw ISO strings are passed to localeCompare instead of comparing parsed epochs, while NaN from Date.parse makes <=, >, and < guards false. Valid offset representations are consequently misordered, and invalid timestamps bypass expiry, freshness, or monotonicity guards.

findings.title: Validate expected receipts before adding them to availability
findings.explanation: Only row.available is validated. A matching receipt with quantity -100 and an arrival before the promise date is summed, producing negative or understated availableByPromiseDate; NaN produces a NaN answer that propagates into canPromise and availabilityRatio. An invalid arrivesAt is silently discarded because NaN <= promiseMs is false. inventory-promise.ts has the same filter-before-validation policy, allowing malformed excluded receipts to evade validation. No constructor or other runtime guard is present in the supplied change.
findings.failurePath: queryAvailability filters receipts solely by Date.parse(arrivesAt) <= promiseMs and reduces receipt.quantity without checking it. Validate every receipt timestamp and finite non-negative safe-integer quantity before filtering by cutoff.

findings.title: Reject malformed reservation metadata and stock snapshots before returning success
findings.explanation: validateReservationRequest validates line quantities and snapshot ownership but never validates requestId, customerId, requestedAt, or snapshot quantities. A request with an empty requestId and a matching snapshot whose available value is Infinity passes validation and fulfillment, and previewReservation returns 201 with an empty identifier and infinite remainingAvailable. This can also produce a malformed reservation URL and event partition key. TypeScript interfaces are not runtime guards, and previewReservation explicitly relies on this validator as its input boundary.
findings.failurePath: previewReservation calls validateReservationRequest; the validator accepts malformed metadata and does not inspect snapshot.available/reserved; isFulfillable accepts Infinity and buildAllocationPlan publishes it in the receipt.

findings.title: Validate the complete inventory event before serialization
findings.explanation: serializeInventoryEvent only checks that lines is non-empty. A directly supplied event with occurredAt="bad", an empty requestId, or quantity=-1 is serialized successfully; quantity=NaN is silently converted by JSON.stringify to null. The exported serializer is the final transport boundary, and neither the interface nor reservationEvent performs complete runtime validation.
findings.failurePath: A nonempty payload bypasses the only guard and flows directly to JSON.stringify, publishing invalid identity, timestamp, and quantity values under the version-1 event contract.

findings.title: Reject duplicate purchase-order lines before indexing them
findings.explanation: new Map(order.map(...)) silently keeps the last line for a duplicate SKU. For order lines [{sku:A, ordered:1},{sku:A, ordered:10}], receiving five units is accepted; reversing those two lines rejects the identical receipt. Purchase-order quantities are also not validated, so malformed previouslyReceived values can distort the limit. The receipt-side duplicate guard does not protect the order input.
findings.failurePath: applyReceipt collapses order lines into bySku before checking uniqueness or quantities, then validates the receipt against whichever duplicate happened to appear last.

findings.title: Validate package and carrier-rate values before selecting a shipment
findings.explanation: The planner validates maximumDays but none of the package or rate numeric fields. A rate with priceCents=-1 and estimatedDays=-1 can be eligible, win the price sort, and produce a negative total price and impossible delivery estimate. Invalid package weights and declared values likewise reach planning or aggregation. The filters only compare these values; they do not establish finite, non-negative integer contracts.
findings.failurePath: planShipment computes the heaviest unchecked package, filters unchecked rates, sorts by unchecked price and duration, and multiplies the selected negative price by the package count.

findings.title: Validate supplier minimum quantities and lead times
findings.explanation: Offer validation covers price and orderMultiple but omits minimumQuantity and leadTimeDays. With minimumQuantity=NaN, Math.max and Math.ceil produce NaN, yet the candidate is selected and returned with NaN quantity and totalPriceCents. A negative or NaN lead time can also win or destabilize tie-breaking. No later guard validates the returned order line.
findings.failurePath: chooseSupplierOffer feeds unchecked minimumQuantity into Math.max/Math.ceil and unchecked leadTimeDays into the comparator, then strips leadTimeDays and returns the corrupted candidate as a valid order line.

findings.title: Keep shipping as an addition to the checkout total
findings.explanation: The existing contract test expects Total(10_000, 1_500, 700) to return 9_200, establishing shipping as a positive charge added after the discount. The new expression instead returns 7_800, undercharging every checkout with positive shipping by twice the shipping amount. This is a direct arithmetic contradiction at the reviewed head; runtime execution was unavailable, but the result is statically deterministic.
findings.failurePath: A checkout passes a positive shipping charge to Total; the function groups shipping with the discount and subtracts both from the subtotal, producing subtotal - discount - shipping instead of subtotal - discount + shipping.

findings.title: Shipping is subtracted from the checkout total
findings.explanation: The changed expression turns the shipping charge into a deduction. For subtotal=100, discount=10, and shipping=5, Total now returns 85 instead of the base behavior's 95. Every reachable caller supplying positive shipping therefore undercharges the order by twice the shipping amount relative to the established formula, causing incorrect checkout totals and revenue loss. The smallest repair is to preserve `subtotal - discount + shipping`.
findings.failurePath: Total evaluates `discount + shipping` first and subtracts that sum from `subtotal`, so positive shipping reduces rather than increases the observable total.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the invoice approval policy
findings.explanation: A session from tenant A that has the `billing-approver` role now passes `canApproveInvoice` for an invoice owned by tenant B. Both tenant identifiers are available at this boundary, and the base implementation explicitly required equality, so removing that comparison makes cross-tenant approval reachable. Restore the tenant match alongside the role check and add a regression test asserting that a cross-tenant approver is rejected and the invoice remains unchanged.
findings.failurePath: `canApproveInvoice(sessionA, tenantBInvoice)` evaluates only `session.roles.includes("billing-approver")`; for an approver this returns true without comparing `session.tenantId` with `invoice.tenantId`, allowing the approval path to proceed across tenant boundaries.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation for invoice approval
findings.explanation: The changed predicate now checks only the role. For a session in tenant A with `billing-approver` and an invoice from tenant B, it returns true. The only approval operation delegates directly to this helper without another tenant guard, so both the exported policy and `approveInvoice` authorize the cross-tenant invoice. Same-tenant approvers still need to pass and users without the role remain denied, but cross-tenant approvers must also be denied. Restoring the shared tenant comparison fixes both affected surfaces. This is confirmed by static control-flow proof; repository execution was unavailable.

findings.title: Preserve the original read error when warning fails
findings.explanation: `Logger.warn` is caller-supplied and its interface does not guarantee that it cannot throw. If it throws here, execution never reaches `throw error`, so callers receive the logging exception instead of the settings-read failure this branch explicitly intends to propagate. Protect the warning call so the original error remains observable.

findings.title: Preserve the settings-read error when warning fails
findings.explanation: The exported Logger contract permits warn() to throw. A valid logger implementation that throws synchronously causes the new catch block to replace the client.read() rejection with the logging exception, obscuring the primary dependency failure and potentially changing caller-side classification or retry behavior. This regression is introduced by the PR and should be fixed at the logging boundary, with a test asserting that the original read error remains the rejection when warn throws. Repository-wide caller inspection was unavailable because the read-only shell sandbox could not initialize, so confidence is reduced despite the direct static control-flow proof.

findings.title: Production file handlers cannot receive their configured INFO records
findings.explanation: Every new `*-production` profile sets `LOG_LEVEL` to `warning` while configuring its file handler at `info`. `load_settings` preserves both values, but this renderer assigns `WARNING` to the root and `service` loggers. Python rejects an INFO record at the logger before consulting the file handler's lower threshold, so the advertised INFO file stream silently loses all INFO records across every production profile. Set the logger threshold to the least restrictive enabled handler level, or otherwise model per-sink thresholds without an earlier global filter. A regression test should apply the rendered configuration and verify that INFO reaches only the file sink while WARNING reaches both sinks.
findings.failurePath: Loading any production profile produces `settings.level == "warning"` and an INFO file handler; `build_dict_config` sets both logger thresholds to WARNING, so an INFO call is discarded before the INFO handler is invoked.

findings.title: Development service records are emitted twice
findings.explanation: Every new `*-development` profile enables propagation. The renderer attaches the same handler IDs to both the `service` logger and the root logger, so a record from `service.accounts` is handled once by `service` and then again by root during propagation. This duplicates every service log line in development and can distort log-based debugging or assertions. When propagation is enabled, attach the sink at only one level; test by applying a development profile and asserting one emitted line per record.

findings.title: JSON profiles emit invalid JSON for ordinary messages
findings.explanation: All new canary, staging, and production profiles select the `json` format, but the formatter is a text template that inserts `%(name)s` and `%(message)s` without JSON escaping. A reachable message such as `user "alice" failed` or any message containing a newline produces malformed JSON, causing structured-log ingestion and parsing to fail. Use a formatter that serializes record fields through a JSON encoder and add assertions that parse emitted records containing quotes, backslashes, and newlines.
findings.failurePath: The logging formatter substitutes the raw logger name and rendered message into the quoted template; embedded JSON-special characters remain unescaped, and the resulting line cannot be decoded as JSON.

findings.title: Production INFO file logging is unreachable
findings.explanation: All ten production profiles set the service/root logger to WARNING while declaring an INFO file handler. Python logging rejects INFO records at the originating logger before dispatching them to handlers, so the file handler never receives the records its lower threshold appears intended to retain. findings.title: Development service records are emitted twice

findings.title: Compatibility wrapper drops previously public constants

findings.title: Preserve lookup failures instead of reporting a closed account
findings.explanation: This catch-all converts every rejected `client.get` call into a successful, fabricated closed-account result. The unchanged contract test explicitly supplies an `Error("upstream unavailable")` and requires `loadAccount` to reject with that same error while logging the warning. The new behavior therefore hides backend outages from the request handler, skips its recovery/error path, and falsely represents an unknown account state as definitively closed. The error-swallowing, fabricated-state, response-contract, and control-flow counterexamples share this single repair boundary.
