findings.title: Account lookup failures are reported as confirmed account closure
findings.explanation: The catch-all handler converts every rejection from `client.get(id)`—including transient network failures, permission failures, and malformed responses—into a successful `{ id, status: "closed" }` result. This prevents every consumer from distinguishing an observed closed account from an account whose state was never retrieved, suppressing caller-level retry and error handling and potentially causing incorrect closed-account reporting or downstream decisions. Logging preserves diagnostics but does not preserve the function's failure contract. The repository caller graph and tests were unavailable because read-only shell inspection failed, so no broader authorization or persistence impact is asserted.
findings.failurePath: For a reachable `AccountClient.get(id)` rejection such as a timeout, control enters the catch block, logs a warning, and returns a structurally successful closed-account value; the awaiting caller follows its normal closed-account branch instead of its rejection/retry path.

findings.title: Do not return 202 after persistence fails

findings.title: Management permission no longer enforces workspace tenant isolation
findings.explanation: `canManage` now checks only `workspace:manage`, and both exported operations stopped supplying the target workspace. Concrete counterexample: an actor whose `tenantId` is B and whose permissions include `workspace:manage` can pass a tenant-A workspace to `readSecret` and receive its secret; the same actor can pass it to `updateSetting` and receive a modified tenant-A workspace. These preconditions are reachable directly through the exported APIs because each accepts an independently supplied `Actor` and `Workspace`. The strongest disconfirming guard would be an upstream tenant-scoping guarantee, but none exists in these functions or the supplied contract, while the base implementation explicitly enforced `actor.tenantId === workspace.tenantId`. The shared repair is to restore tenant comparison in the canonical authorization helper for both read and update surfaces.
findings.failurePath: `readSecret` or `updateSetting` calls `canManage(actor)`; the permission-only predicate returns true without comparing `actor.tenantId` to `workspace.tenantId`; the former discloses `workspace.secret`, while the latter applies the requested setting to the foreign workspace value.

findings.title: Do not convert every account lookup failure into a closed account
findings.explanation: The catch now resolves with a fabricated `{ id, status: "closed" }` for every rejection from `client.get(id)`. For example, a timeout, authentication failure, or upstream 500 becomes indistinguishable from an authoritative closed-account result, so callers can deny access or cache/display false account state while believing the lookup succeeded. Logging does not preserve the function's rejection contract for callers. No error classification or guard in the changed hunk limits this fallback to a documented closed-account condition. Repository inspection was unavailable because the command sandbox could not create its namespace, so confidence is based on the direct static contradiction in the authoritative current-head hunk.
findings.failurePath: `client.get(id)` rejects for a dependency or authorization failure -> the broad `catch` logs the exception -> line 16 returns a synthetic closed account -> the returned promise resolves successfully and the caller cannot recover, retry, or distinguish the failure from persisted account state.

findings.title: Do not convert every lookup failure into a closed account
findings.explanation: The unchanged contract test explicitly requires an upstream-unavailable error from AccountClient.get to reject through loadAccount so the request handler can observe it. This catch now fulfills with a fabricated closed-account record for every error, including outages, authentication failures, and timeouts. That simultaneously breaks the rejection contract and misrepresents unverified lifecycle state; one repair—preserving the rejection or narrowly mapping only an explicitly classified not-found result—covers all counterexamples.
findings.failurePath: When client.get(id) rejects, the catch logs the error and returns { id, status: "closed" }. The loadAccount promise therefore fulfills instead of rejecting, causing the existing assert.rejects contract to fail and allowing callers to process a dependency failure as a successful closed-account lookup.

findings.title: Honor handler thresholds without dropping or duplicating records
findings.explanation: The renderer assigns the global level to both the root and `service` loggers while attaching the same handlers to each. In every production profile, `LOG_LEVEL` is `warning` but the file handler is explicitly `info`; `service.info(...)` is therefore rejected by the logger before the INFO file handler can receive it. Conversely, every development profile enables propagation, so a service record is handled once by the service logger and again by the root logger. This systemically loses intended production INFO file logs and duplicates development logs across all ten services. Derive the logger threshold from the least-restrictive configured handler and ensure each record has one handler-ownership path, with regression coverage for production split thresholds and development propagation.
findings.failurePath: `load_profile` parses the checked-in profile, then `build_dict_config` sets both logger levels from `settings.level` and installs identical handler lists. Production INFO records fail the service logger's WARNING gate; development records reach the service handler and propagate to the same root handler.

findings.title: Preserve an explicitly supplied zero grace period
findings.explanation: The CLI contract permits zero to disable the shutdown grace period, as demonstrated by `test_zero_disables_grace_period`. Replacing the explicit `is not None` check with truthiness collapses zero into absence. Consequently, `resolve_config(0, {"SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS": "60"})` returns 60, while the same call without that environment key returns the default 30. Both counterexamples have the same root cause and are covered by restoring an absence-only fallback.
findings.failurePath: A caller supplies `cli_grace=0`; the `or` expression treats it as false and evaluates the environment/default branch; `WorkerConfig.shutdown_grace_seconds` receives 60 or 30 instead of 0, preventing the requested immediate shutdown behavior.

findings.title: Preserve an explicit zero-second CLI grace period
findings.explanation: `cli_grace` distinguishes `None` from integer values, and the negative-only validation makes zero valid. At the reviewed head, using `or` treats `cli_grace=0` as absent, changing the established CLI-over-environment precedence. For example, `resolve_config(0, {"SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS": "30"})` now returns 30 instead of 0; an invalid environment value can even raise despite a valid explicit CLI value. No guard in the changed function disallows zero. Restore an explicit `is not None` check and add a regression test asserting that zero overrides the environment.
findings.failurePath: A caller supplies `cli_grace=0`; the falsy left operand causes evaluation of `int(environment.get(...))`; the environment value replaces the explicit CLI value (or raises during parsing), and the returned `WorkerConfig` has the wrong shutdown grace.

findings.title: Successful 204 deletes now raise while parsing an empty body
findings.explanation: The removed 204 branch was the only guard preventing body parsing after a successful bodyless DELETE. A reachable response with status 204 has no JSON representation, so `response.json()` raises a decoding error even though the server completed the deletion. The client therefore reports false failure after a successful mutation, potentially prompting unnecessary retries. Restore the 204 return (or otherwise skip JSON parsing for responses without a body) and cover it with a test asserting that a 204 delete returns normally.

findings.title: Do not acknowledge imports whose persistence failed
findings.explanation: The new catch converts every persistence rejection into the same 202 returned after a successful write. This collapses the error-handling, persistence, data-integrity, and response-contract counterexamples into one root cause: callers cannot distinguish a stored import from a failed write, so they may stop retrying while the acknowledged import does not exist.
findings.failurePath: store.persist(id) rejects during an outage, validation failure, or storage error → the catch returns 202 → the caller treats the import as accepted → no record exists for downstream processing and the failure is no longer observable.

findings.title: Do not report acceptance after persistence fails
findings.explanation: When any valid ImportStore implementation rejects persist(id), the new catch converts that failure into the same 202 result returned after a successful write. The declared Promise<void> interface makes rejection reachable, while this function provides no retry, recovery queue, logging, or alternate durable handoff. Consequently, the caller cannot distinguish a stored import from a lost one and cannot initiate its own recovery. This consolidates the breadth ledger's persistence, contract, data-integrity, and logic candidates under one root cause. Static verification uses the authoritative current-head hunk; repository caller inspection was unavailable because the read-only execution sandbox could not initialize, so confidence is reduced accordingly.
findings.failurePath: acceptImport calls store.persist(id); the promise rejects before persistence completes; the catch handles the rejection and returns 202; control therefore resolves successfully with exactly the same observable value as the normal path, suppressing the failure from all upstream error and retry handling.

findings.title: Premature commit leaves failed orders persisted
findings.explanation: `apply_order` is structured as one transaction whose exception handler rolls back both writes, but the new commit makes the order insert durable before inventory is decremented. For a reachable SKU with zero availability (or any failure during the later update), the function raises while the inserted order remains in the database, so persisted order state disagrees with inventory and the reported failure. Moving the commit back after the row-count check is the smallest repair; a regression test should assert that the order row is absent and inventory is unchanged after the out-of-stock exception.
findings.failurePath: Call `apply_order` for an inventory row with `available = 0`: `BEGIN` -> insert into `orders` -> commit at line 19 -> inventory update affects zero rows -> `ValueError("out of stock")` -> rollback has no active transaction containing the insert -> caller observes failure but the order row remains persisted.

findings.title: Keep the order insert and inventory decrement in one transaction
findings.explanation: This commit splits the two writes that the function's explicit BEGIN/rollback block is designed to make atomic. If inventory is unavailable, the order INSERT has already committed before `rowcount` triggers `ValueError`, so the rollback cannot remove the invalid order. On the success path, the inventory UPDATE is now left uncommitted when the function returns, allowing a later rollback or connection close to undo the decrement while retaining the order. Restore the commit after the row-count check so both writes succeed or fail together.
findings.failurePath: Call `apply_order` for a SKU with `available = 0`: the order row is inserted and committed; the conditional inventory update affects zero rows; `ValueError` is raised; rollback only affects work after the commit, leaving the failed order persisted. Alternatively, with stock available, the order commits but the decrement remains pending and can later be rolled back.

findings.title: Preserve the established `next_cursor` response field
findings.explanation: This renames the only serialized continuation field from `next_cursor` to `cursor`. The base implementation establishes `next_cursor` as the response contract, while no compatibility alias or accompanying consumer/schema migration appears in the PR. The contracts and pagination counterexamples share this single root cause: existing consumers can no longer find the continuation cursor and therefore fail or stop pagination despite another page being available.
findings.failurePath: A page with a non-null `next_cursor` is passed to `serialize_page`; the result contains `cursor` but no `next_cursor`; an existing client reading `response["next_cursor"]` raises a missing-key error, or a tolerant client interprets its absence as the end of pagination.

findings.title: Preserve the existing pagination cursor field
findings.explanation: The serializer previously published `next_cursor`, but the current head removes that key and emits only `cursor`. Any existing caller deserializing the established response shape will now see a missing field and cannot request the next page. No coordinated schema version or consumer migration is present in the supplied change. Retain `next_cursor` during a compatibility period, or version the response and migrate every consumer atomically. Repository-wide caller verification was unavailable, which limits confidence.
findings.failurePath: `serialize_page` returns a dictionary without `next_cursor`; an existing consumer reads that field, receives a missing value or raises `KeyError`, and pagination stops after the first page.

findings.title: Numeric coercion collapses distinct valid external IDs
findings.explanation: The validator accepts 1–12 digit strings, including leading-zero forms, but the new Number/string round trip maps distinct accepted identifiers to the same value: `"00123"` and `"123"` both normalize to `"123"`. `indexCustomers` uses this normalized identifier as its Map key, so indexing records with both values overwrites one customer and subsequent lookup cannot uniquely resolve the requested record. This regresses the base behavior, which preserved the trimmed digit string. Preserve the validated string representation, or explicitly reject non-canonical leading-zero inputs before indexing.
findings.failurePath: A record with externalId `00123` is indexed under key `123`; a later record with externalId `123` is indexed under the same key and replaces it, causing lookups for either accepted identifier to return the latter record.

findings.title: Numeric coercion collapses valid external IDs
findings.explanation: The validator accepts leading-zero identifiers, but converting them through Number removes those zeros. Consequently, distinct valid pairs such as "00123"/"123" and "000"/"0" normalize to the same key. indexCustomers has no collision guard, so constructing its Map silently replaces the earlier customer with the later one, losing a valid record. This regression is introduced by the changed normalization helper and should be repaired in this PR.
findings.failurePath: Both records pass /^\d{1,12}$/, normalizeExternalId returns the same string for each pair, and indexCustomers inserts both under one Map key; the second insertion overwrites the first and reduces two customers to one indexed entry.

findings.title: Reject an explicitly empty SERVICE_PORT
findings.explanation: The configuration contract distinguishes an absent value, which selects port 8080, from an explicitly supplied empty value, which must fail validation. The existing `test_empty_value_is_rejected` case supplies `{"SERVICE_PORT": ""}` and expects `ValueError`. This truthiness check instead treats that reachable deployment value as absent and silently selects 8080, potentially binding the service to an unintended port. Keep the default limited to `raw is None`; configured values should continue through integer and range validation.
findings.failurePath: `values.get("SERVICE_PORT")` returns `""`; `if not raw` evaluates true; the function returns 8080 before `int(raw)` can reject the malformed value.

findings.title: Empty SERVICE_PORT now silently selects the default port
findings.explanation: Changing the check from `raw is None` to `not raw` makes an explicitly present empty string indistinguishable from an omitted variable. Previously, `SERVICE_PORT=""` reached `int(raw)` and raised `ValueError`, consistently rejecting malformed configuration; current head instead starts on port 8080. This can hide a broken deployment configuration and bind the service to an unintended port. Preserve the default only for an absent key, or explicitly establish and test blank-as-unset semantics if that behavior is intended.
findings.failurePath: A launcher or caller supplies `SERVICE_PORT` as an empty string; `values.get("SERVICE_PORT")` returns `""`; the new falsey check returns 8080 before integer and range validation can reject the malformed value.

findings.title: Preserve tenant alignment when authorizing workspace management
findings.explanation: The shared authorization helper now checks only `workspace:manage`, consolidating the breadth ledger's authorization, mutation-integrity, and logic candidates into one root cause. A tenant-A actor with that permission and a tenant-B workspace satisfies `canManage`, allowing `readSecret` to disclose the foreign secret and `updateSetting` to return a modified foreign workspace. The exported APIs accept the actor and workspace independently, and the base implementation's explicit tenant comparison is direct evidence that tenant alignment belongs at this boundary. No remaining guard appears in either operation's authoritative current-head hunk.
findings.failurePath: Pass an actor whose `tenantId` differs from `workspace.tenantId` but whose permissions include `workspace:manage`; `canManage(actor)` returns true, so `readSecret` returns `workspace.secret` and `updateSetting` applies the requested value without checking workspace ownership.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the shared authorization helper
findings.explanation: The shared canManage helper now checks only workspace:manage, so both exported operations accept a workspace from any tenant. An actor from tenant A with that permission can read a tenant B workspace's secret or update its setting. Restoring the tenantId comparison in this helper repairs both counterexamples.
findings.failurePath: Pass an actor with tenantId A and workspace:manage together with a workspace whose tenantId is B to readSecret or updateSetting; canManage returns true based solely on the permission, after which the secret is returned or the foreign workspace setting is modified.

findings.explanation: At the reviewed head, the table exercises only attempt 3, while Delay has a distinct `attempt == 0` branch whose contract is to return immediately. No equivalent zero-attempt assertion exists elsewhere. Removing this case therefore leaves the branch completely unprotected: a later change can delay the first attempt while the suite remains green. The remaining attempt-3 case would still pass after a regression that special-cases zero incorrectly while preserving later-attempt behavior, leaving the first-attempt contract unverified. findings.title: Committing the order before decrementing inventory breaks atomicity
findings.explanation: At the reviewed head, `connection.commit()` permanently stores the new order before the conditional inventory update. If the SKU is missing or has `available = 0`, the update affects no rows and raises `ValueError`, but the exception handler's rollback cannot undo the already committed order. The existing explicit `BEGIN` and former final commit establish that both writes were intended to share one transaction. Successful calls are also unsafe with Python sqlite3's default transaction mode because the subsequent update starts a new transaction that this function never commits. Keep the commit after the row-count check so order creation and inventory decrement either both persist or both roll back.
findings.failurePath: Call `apply_order` for an absent or exhausted SKU: BEGIN -> INSERT order -> commit order -> UPDATE affects 0 rows -> raise `ValueError` -> rollback occurs after the order commit -> orphaned order remains.

findings.title: Keep the order insert and inventory decrement atomic
findings.explanation: This commit makes the order durable before stock is validated. If the inventory update affects zero rows, the subsequent rollback cannot undo the already-committed insert, leaving an out-of-stock order persisted. It also creates a crash/failure window between the separately committed operations, and under sqlite3's default transaction behavior a successful inventory update remains pending because the final commit was removed.
findings.failurePath: Call apply_order for a SKU with available = 0: INSERT succeeds, commit persists the order, UPDATE returns rowcount 0, ValueError triggers rollback, but the order remains in the database.

findings.title: Shipping is subtracted from the checkout total
findings.explanation: The change alters the established calculation from `subtotal - discount + shipping` to `subtotal - discount - shipping`. For subtotal 100, discount 10, and shipping 5, `Total` now returns 85 instead of 95. Because this exported helper directly determines the checkout total, every positive shipping charge lowers the amount rather than increasing it, causing systematic undercharging. The authoritative current-head hunk confirms the defect remains present.
findings.failurePath: A caller passes a positive shipping charge to `Total`; the new parentheses group shipping with discount, and the outer subtraction subtracts both values from subtotal, returning an amount lower than the discounted subtotal.

findings.title: Avoid deadlocking when more than one worker publishes a result
findings.explanation: Run waits for every worker before it begins draining results. Each worker must send its result before completing, so the new capacity-one channel allows the first send to finish but blocks the second. That worker never reaches Done, workers.Wait never returns, and the receive loop cannot start. Any input containing at least two jobs can therefore hang indefinitely; retain capacity for all jobs or consume results concurrently.
findings.failurePath: Run receives two jobs -> first worker fills results -> second worker blocks sending -> workers.Wait blocks because that worker cannot finish -> result draining never begins -> Run never returns

findings.title: Capacity-one result channel deadlocks multi-job batches
findings.explanation: The changed channel capacity is 1 while Run launches one worker per job and waits for every worker before draining results. For any input with at least two jobs, the first worker can fill the channel and another worker blocks sending; that blocked worker cannot call Done, so workers.Wait cannot finish and Run never reaches the receive loop. This consolidates BW-001 and BW-002 as one root cause. The empty and single-job cases do not guard the multi-job path, and the original len(jobs) capacity shows the intended pre-wait buffering boundary.
findings.failurePath: Run receives jobs with len >= 2 -> creates results with capacity 1 -> workers concurrently send one Result each -> one send fills the channel and at least one send blocks -> the blocked worker never completes its deferred WaitGroup.Done -> workers.Wait blocks forever -> result draining is unreachable -> caller observes Run never returning.
